Definition: A specimen categorized as “Inadequate/Insufficient/Non-diagnostic” lacks sufficient material, in quantity or quality, for a reliable diagnosis.

An “Insufficient/Inadequate/Non-diagnostic” categorization may result from a variety of technical, preparation, and sampling issues and is defined in relation to the clinical history, physical examination and imaging findings, and fundamentally the material for assessment on the direct smears or in LBC preparation. The reasons why an FNAB is categorized as “Insufficient” should be stated in the report, such as obscuring blood or ultrasound gel, slow drying artefact in Giemsa stains, air-drying artefact in alcohol-fixed Pap-stained slides, crush artefact, lysis of cells due to contamination with local anaesthetic, formalin vapour effect, low cellularity of the sample due to technical difficulties in obtaining material or the nature of the specimen, or poor FNAB technique.

Some soft tissue tumours have abundant collagen, for example desmoid fibromatosis or low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma; this may produce low cellularity {17260203; 17477374}, and CNB is required {35427924; 15918176}. Superficial fat tumours may yield only fat, and myxoid lesions only acellular or paucicellular myxoid background, and correlation with clinical and imaging findings is required.

In contradistinction to an “Insufficient” categorization, any FNAB is adequate if it is diagnostic of a neoplasm or lesion consistent with the clinical setting and imaging findings. If there are any atypical features, even if smears are technically suboptimal, the case is categorized as “Atypical” rather than “Insufficient”. When only benign cells are present, such as fat or skeletal muscle, some cytopathologists categorize this as “Non-diagnostic” if the FNAB target was regarded as a suspicious mass or lesion; others describe and categorize the material on the smears as “Benign” and add a mandatory caveat that “the material may not represent the targeted lesion”. In this the first edition of the WHO Reporting System for Soft Tissue Cytopathology (WHO System), both approaches are acceptable; an institution or cytopathologist should clearly communicate with their clinicians, choose which approach to take, and stick to it. In both scenarios, a repeat biopsy, most commonly repeat FNAB or CNB, is required. Site also influences concepts of adequacy; for example, the differential diagnosis of deeply located, intramuscular, and especially large fatty tumours includes lipoma-like atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma, and the requirement for adequate material shifts not only in regard to the amount and features of the material on the FNAB smears, but also as to the availability of material for studies to determine MDM2 amplification status {32926591}.

The FNAB sample may be “Insufficient”, but a later cell block or other ancillary test may provide sufficient material for a diagnosis. An institution or cytopathologist can decide whether to issue the FNAB report including a statement that ancillary tests are to follow, and then later a supplementary report where the diagnostic category may be changed, or to report the FNAB only once all cell block and ancillary tests are available.

Reported rates of the “Insufficient/Inadequate/Non-diagnostic” category vary widely {12451566; 32926591; 31611506; 32622858}, influenced by the criteria used to define adequacy, the type of procedure, imaging and clinical findings, and the expertise of the person performing the procedure. In a meta-analysis of 13 reports on the adequacy of bone and soft tissue FNAB, the range of adequate specimens for soft tissue lesions was 39–95% {32622858}.

Reports on the ROM for soft tissue FNAB are limited, but the ROM for the “Insufficient/Inadequate/Non-diagnostic” category is often reported as high, most likely due to sampling error. A recent large single-institution retrospective study of 2214 cases showed a ROM of 29.87% for the “Insufficient” category, but it also showed that the ROM for all categories varied with the FNAB cytopathological pattern, from low for lipomatous tumours; to higher for spindle cell, epithelioid, and myxoid tumours; to very high for pleomorphic and round cell tumours {39212584}.

Management of a patient with an “Inadequate/Insufficient/Non-diagnostic” FNAB report requires correlation with the clinical and imaging findings, and repeat FNAB, ideally with ROSE, is required in almost all cases, with or without CNB if available. If the repeat procedures do not yield a diagnosis in cases of clinical and/or imaging suspicion, then CNB (if it has not been performed up to this point) or incisional or excisional biopsy should be recommended. Imaging guidance, which decreases the sampling error, is recommended for all impalpable or difficult to access lesions {35427924}.
